title: What Inspired Means
subtitle: Dictation, verbal-plenary, dynamic, and encounter. Four accounts of how the breath of God became human words.
triageNote: That Scripture is breathed out by God is bedrock. Every view on this page says it. What divides faithful churches is the mechanics underneath the confession, how exactly the breath of God and the pen of Isaiah relate. That question has split seminaries and shaped whole traditions. But it runs between people who all open the same book expecting to hear God in it. Confess the inspiration without flinching. Hold your model of it with some humility. Scripture describes the fact far more often than it explains the method.
question: Paul writes that all Scripture is theopneustos, breathed out by God. Peter writes that men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. Both verses state a fact and neither explains a mechanism. So how did it work. When Jeremiah dictated to Baruch, when Luke interviewed eyewitnesses, when Paul wrote a letter with greetings and a request for his cloak, what was God doing. And what were the men doing. Did God supply the very words. Did He supply the message and let the men find the words. Did He prepare the men so thoroughly that their free words were His words. Or is the Bible the human witness to revelation, the place where God reliably meets us, rather than a book whose sentences are themselves divine speech. Four serious answers have been given. Each one is trying to protect something the others can lose.
whyItMatters:
Open your Bible and look at what is actually there. A love poem. A census. Paul losing his patience with the Galatians. Four Gospels that tell the same story in four voices, with Luke telling you plainly that he did research. A psalm that begs God to break teeth. If God wrote this book, why does it sound so much like people. And if people wrote it, why has it read two thousand years of readers down to the bone.

Your model of inspiration is the answer you give to that double question. And it is not academic. It decides how you read. The reader who assumes dictation treats every sentence as equally direct divine address and gets confused by Luke's footnotes and Paul's moods. The reader who assumes the Bible is merely human testimony starts grading the book. He keeps the parts that read like God to him, which usually means the parts that agree with him. Between those ditches there is a road. The four views on this page are four serious attempts to pave it.

It also decides what you do with the Bible's humanity. The genealogies, the borrowed Greek poetry, the grammar that makes scholars wince in places, the personalities that bleed through every page. One view treats the humanity as a problem to minimize. One treats it as the chosen instrument. One treats it as the proof of freedom. One treats it as the whole point, the creaturely witness God condescends to use. Knowing which you believe will tell you why you read the way you read.

positions.name: The dictation view
positions.inOneLine: God gave the words themselves, and the human writers received and recorded what He said, the way Baruch took down the words of Jeremiah.
positions.bestCase:
I know this view is the one everyone else in this conversation defines themselves against, so let me state it carefully, because what I am guarding is not crude. I am guarding the conviction that when you read the Bible, the words, not just the gist, are God's.

Start with what Scripture shows you. The Lord said to Moses, write these words. The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying, write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you. And Jeremiah called Baruch, and Baruch wrote at his dictation. David says, the Spirit of the Lord speaks by me, his word is on my tongue. The risen Christ in Revelation says to John, seven times, write. Then He dictates seven letters word for word. I did not invent the dictation picture. The Bible paints it, page after page, in its accounts of how prophecy actually arrived. Thus says the Lord is the most repeated claim in the Old Testament. And it is a claim about words.

Now, do I think Luke went into a trance and took shorthand from heaven. No. And the careful men who used dictation language, the Protestant scholastics of the seventeenth century who spoke of the writers as the Spirit's amanuenses, his secretaries, did not think so either. They used the figure to locate the authority, not to describe the psychology. The point of the secretary image is that a secretary adds nothing and subtracts nothing. What stands written is what the Author wanted written, down to the choice of word. If the Spirit chose to produce those words through Luke's research and Paul's temperament, fine, but the product is verbally God's, as truly as if it had been dictated. And I would rather overstate God's control than understate it.

Here is the danger I am posted against. Every softening of the doctrine of inspiration in the history of the church has begun by driving a wedge between the message, which was kept, and the words, which were surrendered. But you cannot keep a message while surrendering its words, any more than you can keep a melody while surrendering the notes. Jesus rested an argument on the tense of a verb, I am the God of Abraham, and on a single word in a psalm. He could do that only because the words themselves carry the authority. That is the treasure in my keeping. Judge the rest of my view by it.
advocates: strands of seventeenth-century Protestant scholasticism (the amanuensis figure)
popular piety in many traditions, more often assumed than argued

positions.name: The verbal-plenary view
positions.inOneLine: God so prepared and superintended the human authors that what they freely and fully wrote, down to the words, was exactly what He intended, without dictation.
positions.bestCase:
The word I want you to learn is concursus, a flowing together. Not God overriding the writers, not the writers performing for an approving God, but one product with two true authors, the way the answer of the tongue is from the Lord even while the plans of the heart belong to man.

B. B. Warfield, who gave this view its classic modern form at Princeton in the late nineteenth century, used to make a point that I think settles the dictation question without losing what dictation wanted. If God needed Paul's letters, He did not wait until Paul sat down to write and then seize the pen. He made Paul. The Pharisee's training, the Roman citizenship, the temperament like a struck match, the conversion on a particular road, every one of these was providence preparing the exact man whose free letter to the Galatians would be the very word of God. The Spirit did not have to bypass Paul's personality, because Paul's personality was itself part of the inspiration. That is why Isaiah sounds like Isaiah and Amos sounds like a herdsman and Luke writes the best Greek in the New Testament. The humanity is not leakage. It is craftsmanship.

Now the two technical words, because they mark the boundaries. Verbal means the inspiration extends to the words, not merely the ideas. Jesus argues from a single word of Psalm 110, Paul argues from a singular noun, seed, in Genesis. Plenary means full, all of Scripture, the census lists and the love poetry along with the Sermon on the Mount, because Paul says all Scripture is breathed out by God, not the religiously useful parts. The 1978 Chicago Statement, in its eighth article, says it in one breath: God in His work of inspiration utilized the distinctive personalities and literary styles of the writers whom He had chosen and prepared, and He did not, in causing them to write, override their personalities.

What am I guarding. Against the dictation instinct, I am guarding the real humanity of the book, because a docetic Bible, a Bible whose humanity is only apparent, dishonors the God who chose to speak through men and not around them. Against the looser views, I am guarding your confidence, because if inspiration covers only the thoughts, then somewhere a fallible human chose the words, and every promise you have ever leaned on stands one translation away from quicksand. Concursus lets me say the whole thing. Every word of Galatians is Paul, all the way down. Every word of Galatians is God, all the way down. I will not give up either sentence.

positions.name: The dynamic view
positions.inOneLine: God inspired the writers and their message, the thoughts and the burden, and the writers clothed that message in their own words, fully adequate and fully human.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin with what I see when I actually compare Scripture with Scripture, because this view was born from reading, not from retreat. Matthew, Mark, and Luke report the words Jesus said at the Last Supper, the most carefully remembered sentences in the church's possession. And they report them with small differences. The inscription over the cross is given four ways by four evangelists. Paul quotes the Old Testament now from the Hebrew, now from the Greek translation, now loosely from memory. And the New Testament writers clearly feel free to give the substance of a saying without reproducing its syllables. If God's method had been to supply the very words, His messengers handled them with a freedom I would never dare use with a dictated text. But if God inspired the message, the men, and the meaning, everything I find on the page is exactly what I would expect.

Augustus Strong, whose Systematic Theology of 1907 taught generations of Baptist pastors, put it this way: inspiration did not always, or even usually, involve a direct communication of the words. Thought is possible without words, he conceded, but the Spirit's gift was the burden, the truth, the message, and the prophet's whole sanctified nature rose to give it voice. H. Orton Wiley, the great Nazarene theologian, called the position dynamical precisely to distinguish the living energy of the Spirit in the writer from the mechanical figure of the secretary. The Spirit moved holy men, Peter says, carried them, and what a carried man writes is truly his own writing, in his own dialect, at his own level of Greek, bearing the unmistakable grain of his own mind.

Do not mistake this for a lower view. I say the message is infallibly God's. I say the Bible is the word of God. And I will not blush to say it. What I refuse is a theory that quietly turns the evangelists into dictation machines. Then it must invent explanations for every variation the theory itself created. My view has no such embarrassments. The treasure is in earthen vessels, Paul says. And the vessel's shape is visible in the pouring. God gave the water of life through real wells, and the water tastes faintly of each well, and that taste is not contamination. It is incarnation, the same divine manner as the Word made flesh, who had a Galilean accent.
advocates: much of the Wesleyan and Methodist tradition
many British evangelicals of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries

positions.name: The encounter view
positions.inOneLine: Revelation is God's self-giving in Jesus Christ. The Bible is the unique, commissioned, human witness to that event. Through it God speaks today as He takes its words into service.
positions.bestCase:
Let me start where you might not expect, with how highly I regard this book. I read it morning and evening. I preached it for decades. I wrote thousands of pages of dogmatics that do almost nothing but exegete it. The Bible is the church's one norm, the witness by which every sermon, every council, and every theology, including mine, stands under judgment. I say all this so you will hear the next sentence rightly. The Bible is not the revelation. The Bible is the witness to the revelation, and the revelation is Jesus Christ.

Think about what the word of God is, biblically. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God, and the Word became flesh. Not became a book. When God spoke His final word, Hebrews says, He spoke in a Son. The prophets and apostles stand around that event like witnesses around a courtroom, and their testimony is irreplaceable, commissioned, the only access we have. Search the Scriptures, Jesus says, for they bear witness about me, and then the terrible second half, yet you refuse to come to me. There were men who had memorized the witness and missed the Word. That possibility is what my whole doctrine is built to name.

So I speak of the word of God in three forms. The Word revealed, Jesus Christ. The word written, Scripture, the prophetic and apostolic witness. The word proclaimed, the church's preaching. The Bible becomes the word of God for you, again and again, as the free and living God takes this human testimony and speaks through it. That is how the preached sermon, fallible human speech, becomes God's address when God wills. This is not a diminishment. It is a description of what actually happens every time Scripture has seized you. The text did not change. God spoke.

What am I guarding. The freedom and personhood of God. A revelation you can possess, bind in leather, and wield is a revelation that has stopped being an act of the living God and become a thing, and things become weapons, and the history of Scripture used as a weapon, against Galileo, for slavery, by the German Christians of my own bitter century, is long. God is not at our disposal, not even between black covers. He is faithful, and He has bound Himself to this witness, and He will speak there, but He speaks as Lord, fresh, free, and never as our possession. Read the Bible expecting an encounter, not consulting an archive, and you are reading it the way I mean.

biblicalEvidence.summary: All Scripture is theopneustos, breathed out by God, and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. Warfield argued at length that the Greek word means breathed out, produced by God, not breathed into, merely enlivened, which makes the verse a statement about origin.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the encounter view, since Paul attaches the divine breath to the writings themselves, the graphe, not to the event of reading them.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The encounter view answers that Paul is describing Scripture's commission and power in the church's life, exactly what the witness doctrine affirms, and notes the verse names purposes, training in righteousness, not a theory of wording. The dynamic view stresses that what is breathed out is Scripture as a whole, its message and burden, with nothing said about word-supply. The dictation view takes breathed out at full strength: what God breathes out is words.

biblicalEvidence.summary: No prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. The picture is the wind in a sail, the word used of the ship carrying Paul in Acts 27. Real men, really speaking, really carried.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for strict dictation, because the men are the speakers, carried but not replaced, and a carried ship still has its own shape, timbers, and wake.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The dictation view replies that a ship carried by the wind goes precisely where the wind takes it, which is the whole point: the destination, the words, are God's. The dynamic view hears its own doctrine, divine impulse and human utterance. The encounter view notes that prophecy here is spoken address, an event of God speaking through men. That is what it says revelation always is.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Dynamic, with verbal-plenary claiming it confidently
biblicalEvidence.summary: Luke explains his method: many have undertaken accounts, he has followed everything closely for a long time, drawing on eyewitnesses and ministers of the word. Now he writes an orderly account so Theophilus may have certainty. An inspired author describes doing ordinary, careful, human research.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Genuinely hard for dictation. A writer taking divine dictation does not need to interview eyewitnesses, and Luke tells us he did.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The dictation view concedes the description and retreats to the product. However the material was gathered, the Spirit governed what was finally written. The verbal-plenary view welcomes the verse as its showcase, providence preparing the historian whose free research yields God's words, concursus in action. The encounter view points out that Luke's stated goal is certainty about the events, the revelation in history to which his book is witness.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The Lord tells Jeremiah to write all the words spoken to him. Jeremiah dictates to Baruch, the king burns the scroll, and God commands it rewritten. And many similar words were added. Here is actual dictation inside the Bible, and a destroyed text restored with additions.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view that denies God ever supplies words, since this passage shows Him doing exactly that, and hard in a different way for dictation, since the rewritten scroll is longer, with words added, suggesting a living process rather than a fixed transcript.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The verbal-plenary view agrees that prophecy often arrived as words and simply denies that this one mode describes Luke or Paul. The modes of inspiration vary while the result, God's words, is constant. The dynamic view notes that even here Jeremiah's own anguish and style saturate the book that bears his name. The encounter view observes that the word of the Lord in Jeremiah is an event that seizes a man, fire in the bones, before it is ever a text.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul distinguishes: to the married I give this charge, not I, but the Lord, and then, to the rest I say, I, not the Lord. He marks the difference between a command of Jesus he can quote and his own apostolic judgment. And later he adds that he thinks he too has the Spirit of God.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for dictation, and pressed against verbal-plenary, because Paul appears to flag a difference in directness within one inspired letter, which a single uniform mode of inspiration would not produce.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The verbal-plenary view answers that Paul distinguishes sources, a remembered saying of Jesus versus his own Spirit-led ruling, not levels of authority. The proof is that he expects both to be obeyed. The dictation view reads it similarly. The dynamic and encounter views take the verse as a window onto inspiration's texture: a real apostolic mind, weighing, distinguishing, fully engaged, and trusted by God with the writing.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus builds an argument on one word of Psalm 110, that David, in the Spirit, calls the Messiah Lord. The force of the argument depends entirely on the precise wording of the psalm and on David speaking in the Spirit.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any view in which inspiration covers thoughts but leaves wording to chance, since Jesus treats a single word as load-bearing.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The dynamic view answers that the Spirit-given message naturally arrives in fitting words, and that trusting a word is not the same as a theory of word-by-word supply across all genres. The encounter view notes that Jesus is doing what the church always does, hearing God speak through the witness of the psalm, the text becoming address in his use of it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life, and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life. Scripture's own stated function is witness. And it is possible to master the witness and refuse the Word.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any account that treats possession of the text as possession of the revelation, since Jesus describes men soaked in Scripture who missed God standing in front of them.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The verbal-plenary and dictation views answer that the failure of the Pharisees was moral, not textual. A perfect witness refused proves nothing against the perfection of the witness. The dynamic view agrees. It adds that the verse defines the goal of all inspiration, life in the Christ to whom the writings point.

weighing:
My judgment, offered loosely, one reader to another.

I find the verbal-plenary view the strongest place to stand, mostly because of how Jesus handles Scripture. He rests weight on tenses, on single words, on the unbreakability of the text. I want to handle the book the way the Lord of the book handled it. And the concursus at the heart of the view, fully Paul and fully God in the same sentence, is the only account I know that takes both authorships seriously without rationing either. It has the further advantage of honesty about variety. It can let Jeremiah take dictation and let Luke do research without panic. The mode varies while the result does not.

But I will tell you what the other rooms have given me. I have been helped in all of them. The dictation instinct, for all its bluntness, guards the holy fear that ought to come over anyone opening this book. And the man who has lost that fear has lost more than a theory. The dynamic view taught me to love the humanity of Scripture. It taught me to actually enjoy that Amos smells of the flock and Luke writes like a physician taking a careful history. I stopped treating the personalities as static over the signal. And the encounter view, which I cannot finally adopt, names something every preacher knows and every theory must account for. There are mornings the text lies flat, and mornings the same text stands up off the page and reads you. The difference is not in the ink. The living God speaks when He speaks.

Where the encounter view loses me is at the wedge it drives between the witness and the word. Scripture's own writers do not speak of the text that way. The psalmist does not wait for the statutes to become God's word, he delights in them as God's word at midnight. So I land here, tentatively: the Bible is the word of God written, every word, through whole and unviolated human authors, and it still takes the Holy Spirit to make a single verse of it burn. Inspiration without illumination reads like a concordance. Pray before you read.
charitableDisagreement:
It would be easy to draw this as a line from faithful to faithless, with dictation at the devout end and encounter at the slippery one. Resist that picture. John R. Rice and Karl Barth would have quarreled all night, but both of them rose in the morning and submitted their preaching to the same Bible, and each was guarding a real danger the other ran. The dictation man is right that words surrendered is eventually a message surrendered. The encounter man is right that a Bible treated as a possession becomes a weapon, and that the church has swung it at the wrong people for centuries. The verbal-plenary man is right that you need both authorships whole. The dynamic man is right that the theory must fit the actual phenomena of the text, or it is a theory about some other book.

So is this a hill to die on. The inspiration of Scripture, its divine origin and total trustworthiness as God's word, sits very near the bedrock. And a church that surrenders it will shortly have nothing to say that the culture was not already saying. But the model, the mechanics, dictation versus concursus versus dynamic gift, is a second-order matter that serious believers have always debated inside the same fellowship. The test I would give you is not which theory a person holds but what he does at the kitchen table at six in the morning. Does he open the book expecting God to speak. The theories are four fences around that one fire. Do not die on a fence.

relatedDebates.note: Inspiration is about how the book came from God, inerrancy about what follows for its truthfulness. The verbal-plenary view generally issues in full inerrancy, the dynamic view often in infallibility of message, the encounter view in reliability of witness. The next page in this set takes up that debate on its own terms.

Behind every model of inspiration stands a doctrine of revelation, what kind of act revealing is. If revelation is God giving information, dictation and verbal-plenary follow naturally. If revelation is God giving Himself, the encounter view follows. The revelation page in this set maps that prior question.

relatedDebates.topic: Illumination and the inner witness of the Spirit
relatedDebates.note: Every view on this page agrees that an inspired text still requires the Spirit's work in the reader. Theology calls this illumination. Where inspiration ends and illumination begins, and how much of your assurance about Scripture rests on each, is its own old and rich discussion.
